claim: Pif1 family helicases are conserved from bacteria to humans.
source: Pif1 family helicases are conserved from bacteria to humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the evolutionary conservation of Pif1 helicases, presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A Pif1 monomer preferentially anchors itself to a 3′-tailed DNA junction.
source: a Pif1 monomer preferentially anchors itself to a 3′-tailed DNA junction and periodically reel in the 3′ tail with a step size of one nucleotide, extruding a loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from single-molecule FRET experiments showing preferential binding to 3' junctions.

claim: A Pif1 monomer periodically reels in the 3′ tail with a step size of one nucleotide.
source: a Pif1 monomer preferentially anchors itself to a 3′-tailed DNA junction and periodically reel in the 3′ tail with a step size of one nucleotide, extruding a loop.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic step size analysis using Γ-distribution fitting of single-molecule data.

claim: Pif1's periodic patrolling activity is used to unfold an intramolecular G-quadruplex (G4) structure on every encounter.
source: This periodic patrolling activity is used to unfold an intramolecular G-quadruplex (G4) structure on every encounter, and is sufficient to unwind RNA-DNA heteroduplex but not duplex DNA.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule FRET time traces showing periodic G4 unwinding patterns.

claim: Pif1's periodic patrolling activity is sufficient to unwind RNA-DNA heteroduplex but not duplex DNA.
source: This periodic patrolling activity is used to unfold an intramolecular G-quadruplex (G4) structure on every encounter, and is sufficient to unwind RNA-DNA heteroduplex but not duplex DNA.
evidence: This is supported by unwinding assays comparing RD31 and DD31 substrates under monomer conditions.

claim: Pif1 repeatedly unwinds G4 DNA, keeping it unfolded, instead of leaving after G4 unwinding or going beyond to unwind duplex DNA.
source: Instead of leaving after G4 unwinding, allowing it to refold, or going beyond to unwind duplex DNA, Pif1 repeatedly unwinds G4 DNA, keeping it unfolded.
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule time traces showing repetitive unwinding cycles.

claim: Pif1-induced unfolding of G4 occurs in three discrete steps, one strand at a time.
source: Pif1-induced unfolding of G4 occurs in three discrete steps, one strand at a time, and is powerful enough to overcome G4-stabilizing drugs.
evidence: This is supported by step-finding analysis of FRET time traces showing four distinct FRET states during unwinding.

claim: Pif1-induced unfolding of G4 is powerful enough to overcome G4-stabilizing drugs.
source: Pif1-induced unfolding of G4 occurs in three discrete steps, one strand at a time, and is powerful enough to overcome G4-stabilizing drugs.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing periodic unwinding in the presence of BRACO19.

claim: Approximately 1% of eukaryotic genes encode DNA or RNA helicases.
source: Approximately, 1% of eukaryotic genes encode DNA or RNA helicases.
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature (Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).

claim: Helicases function in nearly all aspects of nucleic acid metabolism in living organisms.
source: These enzymes function in nearly all aspects of nucleic acid metabolism in living organisms (Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Helicases may have additional functions aside from unwinding duplexes, including protein displacement from DNA and RNA, the unwinding of G-quadruplex (G4) structures, remodelling of chromatin and ribonucleoprotein complexes, promotion of Holliday junction branch migration and the catalysis of a range of nucleic acid conformational changes.
source: it is now evident that helicases, as defined by a series of characteristic sequence motifs, may have additional functions aside from unwinding duplexes, including protein displacement from DNA and RNA, the unwinding of G-quadruplex (G4) structures, remodelling of chromatin and ribonucleoprotein complexes, promotion of Holliday junction branch migration and the catalysis of a range of nucleic acid conformational changes (Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008; Pyle, 2008; Paeschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: The Pif1 helicase family is a group of 5′→3′ directed, ATP-dependent, super-family (SF) 1B helicases.
source: The Pif1 helicase family is a group of 5′→3′ directed, ATP-dependent, super-family (SF) 1B helicases that are evolutionarily conserved from bacteria to humans (Bochman et al., 2010; Paeschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the classification of Pif1 helicases.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs).
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase (Pif1), the prototypical member of the Pif1 helicase family, plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs), processing Okazaki fragments, promoting break-induced replication, maintaining mitochondrial DNA, and preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs (Boule and Zakian, 2006; Bochman et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase plays critical roles in processing Okazaki fragments.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase (Pif1), the prototypical member of the Pif1 helicase family, plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs), processing Okazaki fragments, promoting break-induced replication, maintaining mitochondrial DNA, and preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs (Boule and Zakian, 2006; Bochman et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase plays critical roles in promoting break-induced replication.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase (Pif1), the prototypical member of the Pif1 helicase family, plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs), processing Okazaki fragments, promoting break-induced replication, maintaining mitochondrial DNA, and preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs (Boule and Zakian, 2006; Bochman et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase plays critical roles in maintaining mitochondrial DNA.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase (Pif1), the prototypical member of the Pif1 helicase family, plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs), processing Okazaki fragments, promoting break-induced replication, maintaining mitochondrial DNA, and preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs (Boule and Zakian, 2006; Bochman et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase plays critical roles in preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs.
source: The Saccharomyces cerevisiae Pif1 helicase (Pif1), the prototypical member of the Pif1 helicase family, plays critical roles in inhibiting telomerase activity at telomeres and double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs), processing Okazaki fragments, promoting break-induced replication, maintaining mitochondrial DNA, and preventing replication pausing and DSBs at G-quadruplex (G4) motifs (Boule and Zakian, 2006; Bochman et al., 2010; Lopes et al., 2011; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Pif1 is known to unwind RNA/DNA hybrids better than dsDNA but its mechanistic basis is unknown.
source: For example, Pif1 is known to unwind RNA/DNA hybrids better than dsDNA but its mechanistic basis is unknown (Boule and Zakian, 2007).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The binding constant (KD) of Pif1 to a partial duplex DNA with a 3′ 40-nt Poly(dT) overhang is 7 ± 2 nM.
source: Half of the DNA was occupied by Pif1 at 7 ± 2 nM Pif1 concentration after 2-min incubation
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pif1 dissociation was minimal 30 min after washing out unbound proteins.
source: Pif1 dissociation was minimal 30 min after washing out unbound proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pif1 binding to ssDNA stretches the DNA, resulting in a decrease in FRET efficiency from 0.58 to 0.37.
source: Upon addition of Pif1, a new population with EFRET = 0.37 appeared because protein binding stretches ssDNA (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental FRET data and cited literature on protein-induced DNA stretching.

claim: The average patrolling period of Pif1 on (dT)40 is 2.1 ± 0.1 s.
source: The histograms of the patrolling period, Δt, were nearly identical among all three schemes (>50 molecules each; Figure 1I), yielding an average patrolling period τ = 2.1 ± 0.1 s.
evidence: This is directly measured from experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The KM for ATP in Pif1's periodic patrolling activity is 110 ± 17 μM.
source: Plotting the inverse of τ vs [ATP] and fitting to the Michaelis–Menten equation, we obtained KM = 110 ± 17 μM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is derived from Michaelis-Menten fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pif1's translocation speed is 13 ± 2 nt/s at 20 μM ATP.
source: τ increased linearly with the overhang length (Figure 2C,D), showing that the patrolling is indeed coupled to ssDNA translocation with a speed of 13 ± 2 nt/s at 20 μM ATP
evidence: This is calculated from the linear relationship between overhang length and patrolling period shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pif1's translocation speed is 85 ± 13 nt/s at saturated ATP concentration.
source: showing that the patrolling is indeed coupled to ssDNA translocation with a speed of 13 ± 2 nt/s at 20 μM ATP, corresponding to 85 ± 13 nt/s at saturated [ATP], consistent with previous ensemble studies (Galletto and Tomko, 2013; Ramanagoudr-Bhojappa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is calculated from the Michaelis-Menten parameters and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The kinetic step size of Pif1 ssDNA translocation is 1 nt.
source: The fit yielded n = 26 ± 3, k = 25 ± 3 s−1 for one molecule of (dT)32, suggesting 26 or more steps required to translocate over 32 nt, which supports a 1-nt step size.
evidence: This is derived from Γ-distribution fitting of single-molecule dwell time data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A Pif1 monomer can efficiently unwind 31-bp RNA-DNA hybrids.
source: In contrast, efficient unwinding of RD31 was detected under both conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding curves shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A Pif1 monomer cannot efficiently unwind 31-bp DNA-DNA duplexes.
source: DD31 unwinding was not detectable under the monomer condition but was observed at 100 nM Pif1, likely due to multiple Pif1 proteins acting in concert (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by unwinding curves shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The unwinding time for RD31 by a Pif1 monomer is 6.3 ± 0.9 min at 20 μM ATP.
source: Under the monomer condition, unwinding curves for RD31 can be fit to a single exponential function, yielding the unwinding times tunwind = 6.3 ± 0.9 and 1.6 ± 0.2 min at 20 μM and 1 mM ATP, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of unwinding curves shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The unwinding time for RD31 by a Pif1 monomer is 1.6 ± 0.2 min at 1 mM ATP.
source: Under the monomer condition, unwinding curves for RD31 can be fit to a single exponential function, yielding the unwinding times tunwind = 6.3 ± 0.9 and 1.6 ± 0.2 min at 20 μM and 1 mM ATP, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of unwinding curves shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A Pif1 monomer takes about 200 cycles on average to unwind a 31 bp RNA–DNA hybrid.
source: Our data hence suggest that a Pif1 monomer takes about 200 cycles on average (= 6.3 min/2.4 s) to unwind the 31 bp RNA–DNA hybrid
evidence: This is calculated from the unwinding time and patrolling period.

claim: Pif1 prefers to load at 3′-ss-dsDNA junctions.
source: At 10 nM Pif1, a FRET decrease was observed only for (dT)32+18-S1, whereas at 100 nM Pif1, FRET decreased for both schemes (Figure 4), indicating that Pif1 prefers to load at 3′-ss-dsDNA junctions
evidence: This is supported by differential FRET changes with different labeling schemes shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pif1 is a potent unwinder of G-quadruplexes (G4s).
source: Pif1 is also a potent unwinder of G-quadruplexes (G4s) (Paeschke et al., 2011)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Intramolecular G4 motifs are prevalent in eukaryotic genomes.
source: Intramolecular G4 motifs (four runs of 'GGG', with loops of 1–25 nt between them of any sequence) are prevalent in eukaryotic genomes (gene promoter regions, telomeres, etc) (Bochman et al., 2012)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: G4 formation may slow replication and regulate transcription.
source: G4 formation may slow replication and regulate transcription (Paeschke et al., 2011; Bochman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: G4 structures indeed form in vivo.
source: Growing evidence indicates that G4 structures indeed form in vivo (Lipps and Rhodes, 2009; Paeschke et al., 2011, 2013; Biffi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple literature sources.

claim: Pif1 cannot unwind G4 in the absence of ATP when K+ is present.
source: Addition of 10 nM Pif1 alone did not alter the smFRET histogram of TP-S1 (Figure 5A), suggesting Pif1 cannot unwind G4 in the absence of ATP, when K+ is present.
evidence: This is supported by FRET histogram data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The KM for ATP in Pif1's G4 unwinding activity is 118 ± 7 μM.
source: The average period of the unwinding pattern, τ, depends on [ATP] with a KM of 118 ± 7 μM (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is derived from Michaelis-Menten fitting of experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The (dT)40 region is necessary for G4 unwinding in K+ solution but not in Na+ solution.
source: The (dT)40 region is necessary for G4 unwinding in K+ solution (Figure 5F) but not in Na+ solution (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that the G4 structure is easier to be unwound in Na+ than in K+.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of unwinding activity with and without the ssDNA region in different cation conditions.

claim: Pif1 binding alone may unfold TP G4 in Na+.
source: In Na+ solution, addition of 10 nM Pif1 led to the unwinding of the G4 structure without an adjacent ssDNA region, even in the absence of ATP (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that Pif1 binding alone may unfold TP G4 in Na+.
evidence: This is supported by FRET histogram data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The order of cations' ability to stabilize G4 is K+>Na+>Li+.
source: This is consistent with the known order of cations' ability to stabilize G4: K+>Na+>Li+ (Simonsson, 2001)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Mg2+ facilitates TEL G4 formation both in K+ and Na+.
source: K+ and Na+ titrations with and without Mg2+ indicated that Mg2+ facilitates TEL G4 formation both in K+ and Na+ (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by FRET histogram data at varying cation concentrations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: A Pif1 monomer does not go beyond G4 to unwind dsDNA.
source: Addition of a 21-bp DNA duplex next to the 3′ end of TEL (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) did not affect the periodic G4 unwinding, indicating that even though a Pif1 monomer repetitively unwinds G4 DNA with a very high yield, it does not go beyond it to unwind dsDNA.
evidence: This is supported by periodic unwinding patterns observed with TEL-DD21 substrate shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: PcrA does not efficiently unwind G4 structures.
source: Under monomer conditions (1 nM PcrA) (Park et al., 2010), PcrA showed robust periodic patrolling, but no G4 unwinding was detected (Figure 6C,D). Even at 100 nM, PcrA efficiently unwound dsDNA (Figure 6E), but efficient G4 unwinding was not detected.
evidence: This is supported by FRET histograms and time traces shown in Figure 6.

claim: Having the periodic patrolling activity per se is not sufficient for G4 unwinding.
source: These data suggest that having the periodic patrolling activity per se is not sufficient for G4 unwinding, and robust G4 unwinding is a specific property of Pif1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between Pif1 and PcrA activities.

claim: Robust G4 unwinding is a specific property of Pif1.
source: These data suggest that having the periodic patrolling activity per se is not sufficient for G4 unwinding, and robust G4 unwinding is a specific property of Pif1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between Pif1 and PcrA activities.

claim: G4 unwinding by Pif1 occurs in three discrete steps.
source: Upon close examination of the G4 unwinding phase, we noticed that the FRET decrease occurs in three discrete steps (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by step-finding analysis of FRET time traces shown in Figure 7.

claim: The two intermediate FRET states during G4 unwinding likely represent partially folded states (G-hairpin and G-triplex).
source: The two additional FRET states likely represent partially folded states (G-hairpin and G-triplex), as previously proposed based on ensemble kinetic and simulation studies (Mashimo et al., 2010; Zhang and Balasubramanian, 2012) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data and supported by cited literature on G4 folding intermediates.

claim: G4 refolding occurs rapidly with a refolding time of approximately 0.2 s.
source: The refolding occurred rapidly with a single rate-limiting step (∼0.2 s refolding time, see the Δt5 histogram)
evidence: This is measured from dwell time histograms shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Pif1's patrolling activity is strong enough to unwind G4 structures stabilized by BRACO19.
source: Finally, we found that Pif1's patrolling activity is strong enough to unwind G4 structures stabilized by a small compound, BRACO19 (De Cian et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by periodic unwinding patterns observed in the presence of BRACO19.

claim: The average patrolling period in the presence of 1 μM BRACO19 is approximately 4.7 s.
source: smFRET-time traces of TEL (Figure 7F) and of TP-S1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, Figure 5—figure supplement 7) showed periodic unwinding patterns in the presence of 1 μM BRACO19 with a nearly identical τ value (∼4.7 s; Figure 5—figure supplement 7)
evidence: This is measured from experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: B. stearothermophilus PcrA and E. coli UvrD are both preferentially recruited to 5′-ss-dsDNA junctions and exhibit periodic patrolling with 3′→5′ translocation directionality.
source: Previous single-molecule studies have shown that B. stearothermophilus PcrA and Escherichia coli UvrD, two bacterial SF 1A helicases, are both preferentially recruited to 5′-ss-dsDNA junctions and exhibit similar activities with reverse translocation directionality (i.e., 3′→5′) (Park et al., 2010; Tomko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from previous single-molecule studies.

claim: R-loops occur much more frequently during replication and transcription than previously foreseen.
source: Growing evidence indicates that R-loops occur much more frequently during replication and transcription than previously foreseen, and persistent R-loop formation in cells is a potential source of genome instability including mutations, recombination, chromosomal rearrangements, and chromosome loss (Aguilera and Garcia-Muse, 2012).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Persistent R-loop formation in cells is a potential source of genome instability including mutations, recombination, chromosomal rearrangements, and chromosome loss.
source: Growing evidence indicates that R-loops occur much more frequently during replication and transcription than previously foreseen, and persistent R-loop formation in cells is a potential source of genome instability including mutations, recombination, chromosomal rearrangements, and chromosome loss (Aguilera and Garcia-Muse, 2012).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: It has been proposed that Pif1 inhibits telomerase by unwinding the RNA–DNA hybrid formed between the telomerase RNA and the telomeric DNA end.
source: As it has been proposed that Pif1 inhibits telomerase by unwinding the RNA–DNA hybrid formed between the telomerase RNA and the telomeric DNA end (Boule and Zakian, 2007)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: More than 20 helicases have been shown to bind and/or unwind G4 structures in vitro.
source: Thus far, more than 20 helicases have been shown to bind and/or unwind G4 structures in vitro, among which Pif1 displays the highest specificity in G4 unwinding (Paeschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: Pif1 displays the highest specificity in G4 unwinding among helicases that bind and/or unwind G4 structures in vitro.
source: Thus far, more than 20 helicases have been shown to bind and/or unwind G4 structures in vitro, among which Pif1 displays the highest specificity in G4 unwinding (Paeschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The stabilization energy of a Hoogsteen GG base pair is comparable to that of AT base pair.
source: It has been shown that the stabilization energy of a Hoogsteen GG base pair is comparable to that of AT base pair (Mashimo and Sugiyama, 2007)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The lifetime of G-triplex and G-hairpin could be as long as 0.1–1 s.
source: the lifetime of G-triplex and G-hairpin could be as long as 0.1–1 s, consistent with our observations (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature and is consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: The three discrete steps observed in G4 unwinding are likely due to unraveling of G4 DNA one strand at a time.
source: The three discrete steps observed are likely due to unraveling of G4 DNA one strand at a time (Figure 7D), which indicates that the G4 unwinding by Pif1 is tightly coupled to its translocation activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the stepwise FRET changes observed in the data.

claim: G4 unwinding by Pif1 is tightly coupled to its translocation activity.
source: The three discrete steps observed are likely due to unraveling of G4 DNA one strand at a time (Figure 7D), which indicates that the G4 unwinding by Pif1 is tightly coupled to its translocation activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of discrete steps corresponding to individual strand unwinding.

claim: BRACO19 cannot inhibit Pif1-mediated G4 unwinding.
source: In addition, we also showed that a G4 stabilizing compound, BRACO19, cannot inhibit Pif1-mediated G4 unwinding.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of periodic unwinding in the presence of BRACO19.

claim: Many SF1 and SF2 helicases display limited dsDNA unwinding activity as monomers.
source: Many SF1 and SF2 helicases, including PcrA and UvrD, display limited dsDNA unwinding activity as monomers, and their helicase activity can be greatly enhanced through self-assembly or interactions with accessory proteins (Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The helicase activity of many SF1 and SF2 helicases can be greatly enhanced through self-assembly or interactions with accessory proteins.
source: Many SF1 and SF2 helicases, including PcrA and UvrD, display limited dsDNA unwinding activity as monomers, and their helicase activity can be greatly enhanced through self-assembly or interactions with accessory proteins (Singleton et al., 2007; Lohman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.

claim: The monomeric form of Pif1 is able to unwind RNA–DNA heteroduplexes and G4 structures, whereas dsDNA unwinding requires the binding of multiple Pif1 molecules per DNA substrate.
source: Our data suggest that the monomeric form of Pif1 is able to unwind RNA–DNA heteroduplexes and G4 structures, whereas dsDNA unwinding requires the binding of multiple Pif1 molecules per DNA substrate.
evidence: This is supported by the differential unwinding activities observed under monomer vs. high protein concentration conditions.

claim: DNA binding-induced enzyme oligomerization and/or interactions with accessory proteins might play a role in regulating the translocation vs helicase activity of Pif1.
source: As a result, DNA binding-induced enzyme oligomerization (Barranco-Medina and Galletto, 2010) and/or interactions with accessory proteins might play a role in regulating the translocation vs helicase activity of Pif1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in activity between monomeric and oligomeric forms, and is supported by cited literature.

claim: Pif1 stays in proximity and continually resolves the G4 DNA using its periodic patrolling activity instead of resolving a G4 structure once and leaving the DNA.
source: Instead of resolving a G4 structure once and leaving the DNA, which would allow the intramolecular G4 structure to form again, Pif1 stays in proximity and continually resolves the G4 DNA using its periodic patrolling activity.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of repetitive unwinding cycles.

claim: The inability of a Pif1 monomer to display dsDNA unwinding activity might be important for preventing Pif1 monomers from unwinding dsDNA after the Pif1 monomer has displaced proteins, removed RNA strands or resolved G4 structures from within a ssDNA gap.
source: The inability of a Pif1 monomer to display dsDNA unwinding activity might be important for preventing Pif1 monomers from unwinding dsDNA after the Pif1 monomer has displaced proteins, removed RNA strands or resolved G4 structures from within a ssDNA gap.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed selectivity.

claim: Pif1 performs periodic patrolling on both DD31 and RD31 with an average period of τ = 2.4 ± 0.1 s at 20 μM ATP.
source: smFRET-time traces taken under the monomer condition showed that Pif1 performs periodic patrolling on both DD31 and RD31 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) with an average period of τ = 2.4 ± 0.1 s at 20 μM ATP (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured from experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mg2+ may further stabilize G4 structures in K+.
source: TP G4 formation is evident when [K+] ≥ 60 mM in the absence of Mg2+, or when [K+] ≥ 30 mM in the presence of Mg2+, indicating that Mg2+ may further stabilize G4 structures in K+.
evidence: This is inferred from the shift in K+ concentration required for G4 formation in the presence vs. absence of Mg2+ shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cy3 gets brighter when a protein is in close proximity.
source: To test this hypothesis, we used the fact that Cy3 gets brighter when a protein is in close proximity (Fischer et al., 2004; Hwang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature about the PIFE effect.

claim: Pif1 was purified as previously reported.
source: The S. cerevisiae Pif1 was purified as previously reported (Boule et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological statement citing the purification protocol.

claim: PcrA was purified as previously described.
source: The B. stearothermophilus PcrA was purified as previously described (Niedziela-Majka et al., 2007; Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological statement citing the purification protocol.

claim: All smFRET experiments were performed at 22 ± 1°C.
source: All smFRET experiments were performed with total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy (Roy et al., 2008) at 22 ± 1°C
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental conditions.

claim: The average period of G4 unwinding is close to the average patrolling period of Pif1 on a 3′ Poly(dT) overhang of the same overhang length (71 nt).
source: The average period of the unwinding pattern, τ, depends on [ATP] with a KM of 118 ± 7 μM (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and is close to the average patrolling period of Pif1 on a 3′ Poly(dT) overhang of the same overhang length (71 nt; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured values from different experiments.

claim: Pif1 unwinds G4 with near unity yield on each encounter.
source: The observation indicates that Pif1 unwinds G4 with near unity yield on each encounter.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of periodic unwinding patterns.

claim: PcrA utilizes periodic patrolling activity to dismantle potentially deleterious RecA filaments from 5′ ssDNA ends.
source: In fact, PcrA utilizes periodic patrolling activity to dismantle potentially deleterious RecA filaments from 5′ ssDNA ends (Park et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from the literature.
